common_name: Beverly Hills Apple (Very Low-Chill California-Bred Apple)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Beverly Hills needs only about 300 chill hours, one of the lowest requirements of any apple, making it one of the few apples that can fruit reliably in zone 9 Gulf South winters.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible low-chill pollinator such as Anna, Dorsett Golden, or Ein Shemer. Beverly Hills was discovered as a chance seedling in Beverly Hills, California and remains valued today as one of the lowest-chill apples available, needing only around 300 chill hours, which lets it set fruit reliably even after the mild winters typical of the Gulf South where most standard apple varieties bloom poorly or not at all. Fruit is medium-sized, red-striped, with tart, crisp flesh good for fresh eating and cooking, ripening in mid to late summer. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy for good airflow and fruit quality in humid conditions.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Apple Fact Sheet
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Low-Chill Apple Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Apple Culture for the Gulf South

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; Katy (also sold as Katja), a Swedish cultivar, needs roughly 500 chill hours, moderate enough to perform in some Southern low-chill apple lists alongside Anna and Dorsett Golden.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator. Katy, bred in Sweden and also sold as Katja, produces attractive, bright red, crisp apples with a pleasant, slightly tart, sweet flavor, ripening in mid to late summer, well ahead of most main-season apples. Its moderate chill requirement makes it one of the apple cultivars sometimes recommended for the milder end of Southern apple-growing country, though it needs somewhat more winter chill than the very lowest-chill Florida-bred selections. Thin fruit if the tree sets a heavy crop to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to keep the canopy open for good air circulation.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Apple Fact Sheet
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Low-Chill Apple Varieties
North Carolina State Extension — Apple Cultivars

common_name: Gold Nugget Mandarin (Late-Season Seedless UC Riverside Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Gold Nugget, a University of California Riverside release, is a seedless mandarin that ripens later than most, extending the citrus harvest season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Gold Nugget, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, produces small, bumpy-skinned, essentially seedless mandarins with rich, sweet flavor, notable for ripening later in the season than most mandarins, which extends fresh citrus availability into late winter and early spring. The medium-sized tree is well suited to container culture in areas cooler than its hardiness range. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Citrus Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas

common_name: Tango Mandarin (Seedless Afourer-Type UC Riverside Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Tango, a University of California Riverside release, is a seedless sport of the Afourer/W. Murcott mandarin bred to eliminate the seediness that occurs when the parent variety cross-pollinates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Tango, released by the University of California Riverside citrus breeding program, is a seedless sport of the popular Afourer (W. Murcott) mandarin, bred specifically to stay seedless even when planted near other citrus, unlike its parent which becomes seedy from cross-pollination, while retaining the same rich, sweet-tart flavor and easy-peel skin. It ripens in winter, providing fresh citrus during the cooler months. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season.
sources: University of California Riverside Citrus Variety Collection
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Citrus Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas

common_name: Pixie Mandarin (California Heirloom Seedless Late-Season Mandarin)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root citrus in spring after frost danger has passed, in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Pixie is a California heirloom mandarin prized for staying seedless and ripening notably late, into spring and early summer.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun, protecting young trees from freezing temperatures with covers or by growing in a large container that can be moved in a hard freeze. Pixie is a longstanding California heirloom mandarin valued for small, easy-peel, essentially seedless fruit with rich, sweet flavor, and for an unusually late ripening window that stretches into spring and even early summer, well past when most other mandarins have finished, giving a long tail to the citrus season. The tree tends to be moderately vigorous with a somewhat spreading habit. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing soil to dry slightly between waterings, and fertilize with a citrus-specific fertilizer through the growing season for the best fruit quality.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Citrus Fact Sheet
